title: Chapter 52 — The Albatross
paragraphs: Southeastward from the Cape, off the distant Crozets — a good cruising ground for Right Whalemen — a sail appeared ahead: the Goney, or Albatross by name. As she slowly drew near, from my lofty perch at the foremast-head I had a good view of that sight so remarkable to a newcomer in the far ocean fisheries: a whaler at sea, long absent from home.

This vessel was bleached like the skeleton of a stranded walrus, as though the waves had been fullers whitening cloth. All down her sides this ghostly look was streaked with long runs of reddened rust, and all her spars and rigging looked like the thick branches of trees furred with hoarfrost. She carried only her lower sails. Her long-bearded lookouts at the three mastheads were a wild sight. They seemed to be dressed in animal skins, so ragged and patched were the clothes that had lasted through nearly four years of cruising. They stood in iron hoops nailed to the mast, swaying and swinging over a bottomless sea; and when the ship glided slowly in close under our stern, we six men aloft came so near one another that we could almost have jumped from one ship's mastheads to the other's. Yet those forlorn-looking fishermen, watching us mildly as they went by, never said a word to our lookouts, while below, the hail from the quarter-deck rang out.
"Ship ahoy! Have you seen the White Whale?"

But as the strange captain, leaning over the pale bulwarks, was in the act of putting his trumpet to his mouth, it somehow fell from his hand into the sea; and with the wind now rising hard, he tried in vain to make himself heard without it. Meanwhile his ship was still widening the distance between us. While the seamen of the Pequod were showing in various silent ways that they had marked this ominous incident at the very first mention of the White Whale's name to another ship, Ahab paused for a moment; it almost seemed as though he would have lowered a boat to board the stranger, had not the threatening wind forbidden it. But taking advantage of his windward position, he seized his trumpet again, and, knowing by her look that the stranger was a Nantucketer and shortly bound home, he hailed loudly — "Ahoy there! This is the Pequod, bound round the world! Tell them to address all future letters to the Pacific Ocean! And this time three years, if I am not at home, tell them to address them to ——"

At that moment the two ships' wakes were fairly crossed, and instantly — as was their strange custom — schools of small harmless fish that had been peacefully swimming alongside us for some days darted away with what seemed shuddering fins, and ranged themselves fore and aft along the stranger's flanks. Though in the course of his continual voyaging Ahab must often have noticed a similar sight before, to any monomaniac man the merest trifles capriciously carry meanings.

"Swim away from me, do you?" murmured Ahab, gazing over into the water. There seemed little in the words, but the tone conveyed more deep helpless sadness than the mad old man had ever before shown. But turning to the helmsman, who had been holding the ship into the wind to slow her progress, he cried out in his old lion's voice — "Up helm! Keep her off round the world!"

Round the world! There is much in that sound to inspire proud feelings. But where does all that circumnavigation lead? Only through numberless dangers to the very point where we started, where those we left behind — safe and secure — were all the time ahead of us.

If this world were an endless plain, and by sailing east we could keep reaching new distances forever, and discover sights sweeter and stranger than any Cyclades or Islands of King Solomon, then the voyage would hold promise. But when we pursue those distant mysteries we dream of, or chase in torment that demon phantom which sooner or later swims before every human heart — when we chase such things around this round globe, they either lead us on through barren mazes or leave us swamped halfway.
